warmup.text: Today you meet Jack, who is twelve, and Praiseworthy, the butler. Before you read, a funny poem about a silly voyage in a sieve. Listen for the tone: how sure the travelers sound, and what you can see that they cannot.

words.text: Find the aud and or roots in new words, and spot the phrases that tell where. In the game, weigh six more words. Watch for fool's gold: some words only look like they have a root.

reading.text: Read Chapter 1. Watch for Jack's problem at home and what he wants to do about it. Then look for the moment he chooses his partner. It happens in front of the captain.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapter 1. Then draft your adventure plan in full sentences. Use the frames if you get stuck. Your hero needs one clear problem.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Fix the second sentence in the box.
Tap See the Answer to check.
how.why: A phrase that tells where or when puts the reader in the scene.

do: Read the poem out loud once.
Read the tip about tone.
Answer the question in your reading journal.
how.why: Tone is how a writer feels about the subject. Funny poems show it clearly.

do: Read the question.
Write 2 or 3 sentences in your reading journal.
Then go on to Word Study.
how.why: Thinking before you read gives you something to watch for.

do: Read the phrases from Chapter 1.
Tap the three phrases in the sentence.
Write your own sentence in the box.
how.why: Phrases that tell where help a reader see the scene.

do: Read what aud and or mean.
Type the missing root in each word.
Tap Check It.
how.why: Spotting a root in a new word gives you a head start on its meaning.

do: Say each word out loud.
Tap each card to read its meaning.
Write a sentence with two of the words.
how.why: Saying and using a word helps you keep it.

do: Say each word and find the loud syllable.
Read the Gold Rush words too.
Tap every place name in the sentence.
how.why: Knowing the loud syllable helps you spell the quiet ones.

do: Read the reading focus below.
Open your book and read Chapter 1.
Then do the Read Like a Writer box and the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.
how.why: The pause boxes are places to stop and think while you read.

do: Read the three lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you read. You will use it at the end.
how.why: An adventure has a problem, a goal and a cost. Spotting them helps you follow the plot.
how.use: You will use it in the reading questions.

do: Read today's step.
Turn your plan notes into full sentences.
Use the frames if you get stuck.
how.why: A good plan makes the draft next week much easier.

glossary.meaning: the head servant in a large house
a big difference between two things placed side by side

aud: The hearing root has three letters.
or: The speaking root has two letters.

game.title: The Assayer's Scale
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 words today
game.look: An assayer tested gold in the Gold Rush, to tell real gold from fool's gold. Here you test words. A word with aud (hear) goes on the HEAR pan. A word with or (speak) goes on the SPEAK pan. A word that only looks like one is fool's gold.

do: Read the word on the nugget.
Think about what it means.
Tap HEAR, SPEAK, or Fool's gold.
Tap Next word.
how.why: A root only helps if it is really there. Testing the meaning keeps you from being fooled.

game.doneLine: Come back tomorrow for six more words.

nuggets.why: aud + io + logist: a doctor who tests how well you hear.
No root here. It comes from labor, which means work: a place where scientists work.
nuggets.miss: Is a laboratory about speaking? Look for a smaller word inside.

nuggets.why: or + atorical: sounding like a speech.
No root here. Order comes from a Latin word for a row.
aud + itioned: tried out while someone listened.
or + acle: in old stories, someone who spoke wise words.

art.title: Boston Harbor
art.alt: A painting of Boston Harbor at sunset: a small steamboat with a smokestack and paddle box, tall sailing ships, and the city low on the horizon.
art.look: Fitz Henry Lane painted Boston Harbor in 1854, five years after the novel's ship leaves it. Find the steamboat with its smokestack among the sailing ships. In the novel, the Lady Wilma is both: a sailing ship with paddlewheels and a smokestack.
art.lookBtn: Tap to learn about this painting
art.creator: Fitz Henry Lane

virtue.name: loyalty

options.t: Jack tells the captain, “We're partners, sir,” and picks the coal bunkers over the job of ship's boy.
Praiseworthy keeps Jack's plan a secret and goes with him, paying with his own savings.
Aunt Arabella will not let her servants go: “they are like members of the family.”

virtue.line: Tap the most loyal moment. Then tell why in one sentence.
virtue.placeholder: This is the most loyal because…
